name: Meera

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Meera lives with her parents and two brothers in a rented room. Her mother stitches clothes at home and her father delivers parcels. Their work brings roughly ₹8,000–₹12,000 into the household in a month, before rent and other expenses. Her mother can read Hindi and checks the school diary, but English homework often needs help neither parent can provide.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She reads familiar Hindi passages slowly and understands spoken explanations better than new English text. Her attendance is regular. She spends a long time rewriting answers neatly, sometimes without understanding every word. Her average hides the difference between remembering an answer and explaining it herself.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She enjoys making paper decorations and helps her brothers organise their books. Her mother makes time to listen to her read, but needs material at a level they can work through together.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Meera continues attending after transfer. She begins asking more questions in Hindi. Some understanding becomes easier to notice, while English reading still needs deliberate practice.

update: Meera is still attending. Her family continues reading with her, but has asked for work they can help her understand rather than only check for completion.

name: Dev

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Dev lives with his parents and grandmother. His father repairs bicycles and his mother sells vegetables. Household income is roughly ₹9,000–₹13,000 a month and depends on sales and repair work. His grandmother makes sure he leaves for school, while his parents are usually working when he returns.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He reads short passages and calculates confidently, but rushes through instructions. At home he practises questions from an older cousin’s notebook. Similar exam questions go well; unfamiliar ones are harder. His marks do not show how much help he had with the practice.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He draws bicycle parts and likes explaining how a brake works. His cousin can help on some weekends, but there is no regular time for discussing work he has misunderstood.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Dev stays enrolled after the transfer. He is upset about leaving his friends. A new teacher notices his interest in repairs and asks him to explain a diagram; his adjustment takes time.

update: Dev’s attendance remains regular. He has found someone to build models with, though he has stopped showing his report card around at home.

name: Anjali

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Anjali lives with her mother, father and younger sister. Her father drives a hired vehicle and her mother does tailoring. Around ₹10,000–₹14,000 is available in a working month. Both parents read Hindi, and an older cousin sometimes helps with English. There is a shared table for homework after dinner.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has attended the same school for several years. Her strong marks reflect steady attendance and repeated practice, alongside help at home. She finds it difficult to admit when she does not understand something because adults often describe her as the child who manages on her own.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She writes little stories and enjoys showing her sister how to form letters. Support exists, but being asked what she finds hard would give a more complete picture than congratulating the average alone.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Anjali joins the new section and keeps attending. She worries that the transfer means her earlier work no longer counts. Her reading remains strong; she needs time to trust the new setting.

update: Anjali continues studying. She has asked why she was moved despite completing her work. The office has no answer beyond the review instruction.

name: Ravi

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Ravi lives with his parents, an older sister and a younger brother in a rented room. His father loads goods wherever he can get work. His mother takes occasional cleaning work. Their combined earnings vary between roughly ₹6,000 and ₹9,000 a month. Some weeks there is work every day. In others, the family borrows to cover food and rent.

They have moved twice in the past year as work and housing arrangements changed. Ravi has changed schools with them. His older sister helps the younger children when she can, but she also has schoolwork and household jobs. Neither parent can read the English instructions in his books. There is no money set aside for tuition.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: Ravi recognises some letters and familiar words, but cannot independently read a short paragraph. During one move he missed several weeks. When he joined the next class, lessons were already underway. He learnt to copy what was on the board without understanding much of it.

His notebook can look complete. In a written assessment he cannot use it as a guide, and the gaps become visible. He sometimes interrupts a reading lesson with a joke or an argument. That behaviour needs attention, but it does not explain what he was taught, what he missed or what he can currently read.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: Ravi likes taking apart broken toys and working out how the pieces fit. Other children bring him stuck zips and loose wheels. He is patient with those problems, even when he is impatient in class.
A neighbour sometimes helps him read a few Hindi words. It is occasional help, not a regular lesson. There has been no sustained plan to teach the reading skills he missed across schools.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Ravi joins the Hindi-medium section. He understands more of the spoken instructions, but changing the language does not fill the earlier gaps. He continues attending and copying from the board. At the next review, his books are full. He still needs someone to start with what he can read, rather than the page his class has reached.

update: Ravi’s notebook is still being completed. A later note asks for an individual reading check; the register does not yet record whether that support happened.

name: Sana

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Sana lives with her parents, two siblings and an aunt. Her father sells fruit from a cart and her mother helps with sorting and selling. Roughly ₹7,000–₹10,000 comes into the household each month. An aunt can supervise homework, but cannot explain English exercises. Evenings are busy and books share space with supplies.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has missed school during family moves between rented rooms. She understands basic number work when the question is explained, but has trouble working out what an English worksheet asks. Copying a completed example often looks like independent work until the wording changes.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She remembers prices and enjoys arranging objects by shape and size. She asks for help quietly and can be missed in a crowded class. She needs regular checks that she understands the instruction before starting.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Sana continues in the new section. Some instructions become clearer. The gaps from missed lessons remain, and she still needs teaching that starts with the skills she currently has.

update: Sana is attending. She follows more spoken instructions, while the written reading tasks remain difficult. No regular catch-up arrangement is recorded.

name: Kabir

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Kabir lives with his parents and older brother. His father paints buildings and his mother packs goods through occasional home-based work. Combined income varies around ₹8,000–₹12,000 a month. The family sometimes moves temporarily when a job is far away. His brother helps when he is not studying or working.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: Kabir can read short texts, but changes in attendance have made his progress uneven. A new teacher may see a completed notebook without knowing which lessons someone helped him copy. He does better on rehearsed exercises than on questions asking him to explain his reasoning.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He builds small models from discarded packaging and likes working with other children. There is someone willing to help at home, but no dependable plan for catching up after a move.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Kabir starts in the new section and keeps his model-making friends. He continues attending, but another family work trip interrupts lessons. The section label alone does not explain the next set of marks.

update: Kabir has missed lessons during another family work trip. His classmates have kept the copied pages; the office has no record of replacement teaching.

name: Pooja

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Pooja lives with her parents, brother and grandfather. Her mother cooks in a canteen and her father works at a printing shop. Income is roughly ₹10,000–₹13,000 a month. Both parents can read Hindi. Her grandfather listens while she practises, although he is unable to help with much English.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has a fairly steady school history and strong recall. Her marks are higher when questions resemble exercises she has practised. She can explain some ideas in Hindi but hesitates in English, which can make her appear less sure of a concept than she is.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes performing poems and making signs for family occasions. She has encouragement and a reading partner. She would benefit from room to explain an answer in her own words, not just reproduce it.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Pooja remains in school after transfer. She performs a poem at a class activity and begins settling in. Leaving her previous section still feels like losing recognition for work she had done.

update: Pooja is attending and took part in a class poem. She still needs opportunities to explain new work in her own words.

name: Aman

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Aman lives with his parents and younger brother. His father is an electrician’s assistant and his mother runs a small stitching service. Around ₹11,000–₹15,000 is available in a typical working month. They share a room but reserve a corner for the children’s books. A relative helps with difficult homework.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has attended consistently and practises regularly. His high marks show real progress, but also access to time and help that the register does not record. He sometimes hides mistakes rather than ask a question because he is used to being praised for finishing first.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes puzzles and helps his brother sound out words. He has several adults who support study. A classroom where mistakes are ordinary would help him ask for assistance before a gap grows.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Aman continues studying in the new section. He is confused by the transfer despite his marks. His family asks about it, and the teacher helps him find his place without promising that changing sections has no effect.

update: Aman remains enrolled. His family asked how the decision was reached, and whether support in English will continue in the new section.

name: Neha

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Neha lives with her mother, father and three siblings. Her mother works in domestic cleaning and her father finds occasional warehouse shifts. Household earnings vary around ₹6,000–₹9,000 a month. The older children share care and cooking. Neither parent is comfortable reading the school’s written English messages.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has missed lessons when an adult could not manage the school run. She recognises common words but struggles with a fresh passage. Work sent home for completion does not come with the explanation she missed. The following lesson assumes she caught up.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She enjoys drawing clothing and remembers songs after hearing them once. An older sister wants to help but has learning gaps of her own. Neha needs teaching time, rather than simply more unfinished work.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Neha keeps attending after transfer. Her sister begins walking with her more regularly. Attendance becomes steadier, while the reading she missed still requires specific support.

update: Neha is arriving more regularly with her sister. The attendance change is visible; the reading she missed still needs attention.

name: Imran

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Imran lives with his parents and younger sister. His father repairs shoes and his mother prepares food for a small local seller. Their household receives roughly ₹7,000–₹10,000 a month. A missed day of work changes what can be bought that week. His parents read a little Hindi but cannot explain most English homework.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He can work through familiar sums and reads slowly. He loses marks when instructions contain words he does not know. He rarely asks during an exam because he thinks asking means he has already failed. There is no routine record of what he can explain orally.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He enjoys sketching vehicles and remembering routes through the neighbourhood. His father checks whether homework is done, but needs help understanding whether copied answers mean the lesson was learnt.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Imran attends the new section. He begins explaining some answers in Hindi and asks for clarification more often. He still needs practice reading independently, and his family’s work remains irregular.

update: Imran has begun asking for instructions to be explained. The school has not yet separated what he can calculate from what he can read.

name: Kavya

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Kavya lives with her parents, grandmother and younger sister. Her mother is a shop assistant and her father does repair work. Roughly ₹10,000–₹14,000 comes into the household each month. Her grandmother supervises afternoons. The adults can read Hindi, and a cousin helps with English when visiting.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has a consistent school history and strong memory for written examples. She finds new problems harder than rehearsed ones, particularly if they require several steps. Her average does not reveal which answers she understands and which she remembers by shape or wording.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes making lists and creating pretend lessons for her sister. She has support at home. Being asked to explain how she reached an answer would help reveal the next thing to teach.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Kavya continues studying after transfer. She misses her old group but gradually joins another. Her next teacher asks for explanations alongside answers, revealing strengths and gaps the previous average did not separate.

update: Kavya is attending. Her new teacher reports that rehearsed exercises go well, while unfamiliar problems still need discussion.

name: Rohan

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Rohan lives with his parents and older sister. His father works at a hardware shop and his mother does tailoring. Earnings are roughly ₹10,000–₹14,000 a month. His sister is in school and often sits with him in the evening. They can usually find time for homework even though space is shared.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He reads comfortably and gets strong marks. He has also benefited from staying at one school and having someone explain missed work. He avoids activities requiring speaking to the whole class. A written result does not capture everything that helps or troubles him at school.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He enjoys building card games and making rules for them. His sister gives him patient help. He needs that same permission to think aloud and make mistakes in front of others.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Rohan remains enrolled after transfer. The work is not his main difficulty at first; rebuilding familiar relationships is. He keeps making games and slowly finds classmates who want to play.

update: Rohan remains enrolled. He has started sharing a game with new classmates. No further learning assessment has reached the office.

name: Tara

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Tara lives with her mother, grandmother and four-year-old brother. Her mother cleans in several homes, leaving early and returning at different times. The household receives roughly ₹5,000–₹7,000 a month from that work. Losing a household client means losing part of that income. Paying for childcare or tuition would have to come out of the same money used for rent and food.

Her grandmother has difficulty walking and cannot always take her brother out. Tara washes him, helps him eat and waits until a neighbour can watch him. On those mornings she arrives late. When the neighbour cannot help, she misses school. Her mother wants both children to study, but cannot routinely leave work without risking the job.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: Tara speaks confidently about stories she has heard. Reading them herself is much harder. She can recognise common words, but struggles to follow a new passage independently.

She misses parts of the week rather than a single long stretch. That makes the gaps easy to overlook: she is present often enough to receive the next worksheet, but not always the explanation that came before it. Missed work is usually sent home to complete. Her mother and grandmother cannot read the exercises well enough to teach them. The unfinished pages come back.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: Tara tells her brother stories, changes the endings and gives each character a different voice. She remembers long sequences of events and enjoys explaining them to other children.

A classmate shares notes when she is absent. Copying those notes helps her keep a notebook, but does not replace being taught. There is no reliable childcare arrangement or planned time at school for catching up.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Tara moves sections. The same morning responsibilities continue. Later, her family arranges for her brother to leave with another household, and her attendance improves. She now hears more of the lessons, but still needs help with what she missed. The change that gets her through the school gate does not, by itself, catch her up.

update: Tara’s attendance has improved with a different school-run arrangement. There is still no catch-up plan in her file for the lessons she missed.

name: Mohit

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Mohit lives with his parents and two younger children. His father works as a security guard and his mother cleans homes. Around ₹8,000–₹11,000 is available in a month, with changing shifts. Mohit often waits with his siblings until an adult returns. Neither parent can reliably help with English worksheets.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He knows many letters and reads short familiar lines, but guesses at longer words. He has learnt to copy neatly, which can disguise the effort involved in reading. Some mornings he is tired after interrupted sleep in a shared room. The exam captures his work that day, not the nights before it.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes organising playground races and gets younger children involved. A neighbour sometimes checks his work. He needs consistent reading practice with someone who can notice errors and explain them.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Mohit continues attending in the new section. The household shifts remain difficult. His teacher begins checking a short passage with him each week; progress is uneven rather than immediate.

update: Mohit is attending. A teacher has started short reading checks, but changing work shifts at home still affect his sleep.

name: Nisha

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Nisha lives with her parents, aunt and two cousins. Her mother and aunt make garments at home; her father drives a delivery vehicle. Income available to the household is around ₹9,000–₹13,000 a month. Work materials fill much of the room, and the children wait until the evening to spread their books out.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has attended regularly but has difficulty with long written instructions. She does better when a teacher breaks a task into steps. At home, adults can check some Hindi work but not English. Extra worksheets have increased the time spent working without always resolving the misunderstanding.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes designing patterns and counting repeated shapes. Her aunt notices her persistence. Short explanations followed by a chance to try independently would be more useful than assuming she has not practised.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Nisha joins the new section and remains in school. A different teacher gives shorter instructions and checks the first answer with her. Some work improves, while longer reading tasks remain hard.

update: Nisha has begun completing more tasks when instructions are broken into steps. Her file does not yet show how consistently this help is available.

name: Yusuf

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Yusuf lives with his parents, grandfather and brother. His father runs a small repair counter and his mother takes sewing orders. Roughly ₹9,000–₹13,000 is available in a month. His grandfather reads with him in Hindi. English homework is checked by an older neighbour when that neighbour has time.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He is comfortable with familiar reading and calculations. He has had fewer breaks in schooling than some classmates. His strongest papers follow a period of regular help; his weaker work often involves unfamiliar vocabulary rather than a new mathematical idea.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He makes paper models and likes finding out how household objects work. He has adults willing to help, but the English support is informal. Asking which part he cannot understand would make that support more precise.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Yusuf keeps attending after transfer. He can follow more spoken instruction, but wants to continue learning English too. His family tries to keep both forms of practice going.

update: Yusuf is attending. His family wants both clearer classroom explanations and continued English practice; the transfer itself supplies neither plan.

name: Isha

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Isha lives with her mother, father and younger brother. Her mother is an assistant in a small office and her father repairs electrical equipment. Their earnings are roughly ₹11,000–₹15,000 a month. They make regular time for study and can read school messages. A family member lends her storybooks.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She reads independently and has strong written results. She has remained at the same school. She worries about anything below her usual mark and sometimes refuses to try a task unless she is sure she can finish it correctly. The average records achievement, not the pressure she attaches to it.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes writing captions for drawings and explaining stories to her brother. Reliable books and adult attention have helped. She also needs reassurance that needing help does not cancel what she has learnt.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Isha continues studying after transfer. She initially treats it as proof she has disappointed everyone. Conversations with her family and teacher help, but the loss of confidence does not disappear overnight.

update: Isha remains enrolled. Her family reports that she is worried about making mistakes. She continues borrowing books while adjusting to the new class.

name: Vivek

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Vivek lives with his parents, two brothers and grandmother. His father works on construction sites and his mother sorts and packs goods. Household earnings vary around ₹6,000–₹9,000 a month. Work has taken the family to different rented rooms. Older siblings help with younger children and sometimes with paid work.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has changed schools more than once. He recognises numbers and some words, but cannot follow much of an English passage alone. When a school admits him into his age group, the lesson begins where the class is, not where his previous teaching stopped.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes drawing buildings and notices how objects fit together. One brother can help with elementary sums. He needs someone to establish his current reading skills and teach from that point over time.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Vivek remains at school after transfer. He understands more of the explanations but still copies reading exercises. His school history continues to matter even when the section on his record changes.

update: Vivek is attending, but still copies work he cannot read independently. The record of his earlier school changes has not become a teaching plan.

name: Farah

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Farah lives with her mother, father and two sisters. Her mother cleans offices and her father sells snacks. The household receives roughly ₹7,000–₹11,000 a month. The sisters share cooking and homework space. Her parents can read some Hindi but rely on others for English messages.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She reads familiar text and can solve basic sums, but misses lessons when the family cannot arrange care for her youngest sister. On return, she is given the pages completed during her absence. Copying them fills the notebook without necessarily recovering the explanation.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She enjoys singing and remembers sequences well. An older sister helps when possible. She needs a way back into a missed lesson and a reliable arrangement that lets her attend.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Farah continues attending in the new section. The family finds occasional help with childcare. Her attendance improves for a while, but the arrangement is fragile and the missed learning still needs attention.

update: Farah’s attendance has improved for now. The childcare arrangement depends on a neighbour being available and could change again.

name: Arjun

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Arjun lives with his parents and grandfather. His father works at a small factory and his mother cooks for nearby households. Combined earnings are around ₹10,000–₹14,000 a month. His grandfather reads Hindi and follows the school diary. English practice depends on a cousin’s visits.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He works steadily and has fairly strong results. He finds it hard to explain answers that he has memorised. When an exam changes the wording, he sometimes applies the wrong method. A single total does not show the difference between recall and understanding.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes sketching machines and asking how they work. His grandfather gives him time and attention. Having to demonstrate a method with objects could reveal understanding that an answer sheet misses.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Arjun stays in school after transfer. He begins working with different classmates and continues practising. The change does not erase either his earlier learning or his remaining difficulties.

update: Arjun is attending. An oral explanation of a model revealed understanding not visible in one written answer. His teacher has asked for more such checks.

name: Ritu

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Ritu lives with her parents and younger sister. Her father works in a warehouse and her mother runs a small ironing service. Income is roughly ₹10,000–₹13,000 a month. Both adults can check basic Hindi work. Her sister shares a study space, and the family tries to keep evenings free for schoolwork.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has attended consistently and learns well from examples. She reads short texts independently. She rarely asks questions when confused, preferring to copy a familiar pattern and hope it fits. Strong marks can make it easy to assume she never needs a different explanation.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She enjoys drawing comics and creating dialogue for them. She has support at home. A teacher asking her to talk through an unfamiliar task would show more than a rank in the class.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Ritu joins the new section and keeps drawing. She misses her friends and initially speaks less in class. A later teacher uses one of her comics as a reading activity, helping her take part again.

update: Ritu is still drawing comics and attending school. A class activity has helped her speak more, but the move remains upsetting.

name: Sameer

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Sameer lives with his parents, younger sister and grandfather. His parents run a small tea stall. After ingredients, fuel and other work expenses, the money available to the household is roughly ₹7,000–₹11,000 in an ordinary month. A good day's sales are not the same as a steady monthly salary.

His grandfather needs help getting around. Sameer sometimes watches the stall while an adult buys supplies or takes his grandfather somewhere. He serves customers, counts change and remembers who has paid. At busy times, an afternoon's help turns into most of the evening. Homework gets pushed back.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: Sameer can add and subtract familiar amounts aloud. He struggles when an English word problem asks him to identify what calculation is needed. He can read some Hindi text slowly, but has had little individual help with English reading.

His written maths mark combines several things: calculation, reading the question, understanding the instruction and completing the paper in time. The register shows one number. It does not show which part caused difficulty.

His parents completed a few years of school. They can help with some basic sums but cannot explain much of his current English work. Paid tuition would reduce the money available for household expenses.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: Sameer organises cricket games and remembers everyone's runs. He likes being trusted with a job. At the stall, he gets an immediate response when he does something useful. At school, he often waits for work he cannot begin alone.

There has been no regular assessment separating what he understands orally from what he can read on the exam paper. His practical arithmetic is a starting point for teaching, not evidence that he has mastered the whole maths curriculum.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: After the transfer, some written instructions become easier to understand. Then his father is unable to work for several weeks. Sameer spends more time at the stall. School absences accumulate, and by the following review he is no longer attending. The family still talks about sending him back. That requires a way to manage the work and help him return, not simply another name on the register.

update: Sameer’s absences have continued while his father is unable to work. His family talks about returning him to school; no return arrangement is recorded.

name: Jyoti

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Jyoti lives with her mother, father, grandmother and younger brother. Her father takes temporary shop work and her mother cleans homes. Earnings range around ₹7,000–₹10,000 a month. Her grandmother can supervise the children but cannot read their books. Tuition is not part of the household budget.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has stayed enrolled but reads slowly. She can solve a familiar maths exercise when the instruction is explained, then struggle when the same idea is written differently. In a large class, a quiet child who keeps copying may appear to have understood.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes arranging little performances with her brother and remembers dialogue. Her family encourages attendance. She needs a regular chance to read aloud privately and ask questions without having to interrupt the whole class.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Jyoti continues at school after transfer. Some instructions are easier to follow. A teacher begins checking her first answer before leaving her to work; the extra attention helps identify what she has missed.

update: Jyoti is attending. Checking her first answer has helped reveal misunderstood instructions, but she still needs regular reading practice.

name: Nikhil

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Nikhil lives with his parents and older sister. His father repairs appliances and his mother works at a food stall. Household income is around ₹8,000–₹12,000 a month. His sister is still in school and helps when she can. Evening noise makes it difficult to concentrate, especially while customers are nearby.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He reads familiar passages but needs more time with new material. His calculations are stronger than his written explanations. He sometimes stops attempting a task after misunderstanding the first instruction. The unfinished paper records that stopping point without explaining it.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes taking objects apart and drawing the parts. His sister checks basic work but cannot always explain English. He needs to practise starting an unfamiliar task, with support that can gradually be removed.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Nikhil remains enrolled after transfer. He understands some tasks more readily, though he still works slowly. Time and clear instructions matter more than the new label on the class register.

update: Nikhil is attending and working slowly. He has begun asking for the first instruction to be explained instead of leaving the whole task blank.

name: Asha

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Asha lives with her parents and two younger siblings. Her father works in a workshop and her mother does tailoring. Earnings are roughly ₹10,000–₹14,000 a month. Her mother reads Hindi and makes time for schoolwork. Asha sometimes helps her siblings before beginning her own homework.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She has fairly consistent attendance and strong recall. She can read independently, although new English vocabulary slows her down. Her marks are not only a measure of effort; they also reflect years of relatively steady access to school and help.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes making picture books from folded paper. She can explain stories aloud and enjoys sharing them. She has useful support, but needs time for her own learning rather than always being the person helping others.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Asha continues attending after transfer. Helping new classmates gives her a place in the group. Her teacher also needs to notice when being helpful takes time away from her own work.

update: Asha is attending and helping classmates. Her teacher has noted that she also needs time and support for her own work.

name: Karan

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Karan lives with his parents and brother. His mother works at a shop and his father handles deliveries. Around ₹11,000–₹15,000 is available each month. Both parents read Hindi and some English. They can usually help him practise and contact the school when something is unclear.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has strong marks and a stable school history. He has benefited from reliable attendance, books and someone noticing unfinished work. He can still struggle when asked to explain a method rather than reproduce it. His position in a ranking does not reveal that difference.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes drawing mazes and inventing games for his brother. He has adults who make room for those interests. Opportunities to try unfamiliar problems would help him beyond the next examination.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Karan stays in school after transfer. His parents ask for an explanation. He remains capable of the work, but needs help understanding a decision that does not match how he thought the school valued him.

update: Karan continues studying. His family asked why a strong mark did not keep his place. The office recorded the question but no explanation beyond the quota.

name: Hina

update: Hina remains enrolled. She understands more of the discussion but still needs teaching in basic reading; moving her did not provide it.

name: Deepak

update: Deepak is attending. His route drawings have given the teacher a starting point for explanations, but the missed lessons still need to be revisited.

name: Adil

name: Rekha

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She reads independently, attends regularly and has very strong marks. She has also had continuity: the same school, adults who notice difficulties and a place to keep her materials. Those conditions are not visible beside her average. She can become upset by small mistakes.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes writing stories and helping her sister practise. Her family supports her interests. She needs space to learn something difficult without feeling she has to protect the label of being the best.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story

update: Rekha continues to learn, but the decision has affected her confidence. Her new teacher is making time for questions rather than relying on the high average.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story

name: Zoya

report.title: School and learning

report.title: Later, in this fictional story

name: Varun

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has mostly steady attendance and good recall. He finds it harder to apply familiar methods when a question uses a new example. His average does not show which concepts he could explain without a memorised sentence.

update: Varun remains enrolled. Discussing a model showed both understanding and memorised steps. His next teaching needs are clearer than his average alone suggested.

name: Payal

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Payal is the youngest of four children. Her father works on construction sites. Her mother cleans in several homes. Their combined earnings range from roughly ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 a month, depending on available work. Rent, food and travel have to be paid from that income. There is no separate budget for private tuition.

The family shares one rented room. Two older siblings have already started working to contribute to household expenses. The third is still in school and does much of the cooking and care when the parents are out. Neither parent can read or write. They want Payal to study, but cannot sit with her and explain a worksheet they cannot read themselves.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: Payal has changed schools as her father's work has taken the family to different places. In one earlier placement, her class went through stretches without regular teaching when the teacher was absent. There was no consistent replacement or follow-up for the lessons missed.

She learnt to copy letters before she understood how to read words. Now she can reproduce familiar writing and some memorised answers, but cannot independently read a short passage or write a sentence expressing her own thought. That is different from leaving every exam answer blank: copying and memorised responses can still earn marks without showing independent reading and writing.

The current lessons assume skills she has not yet acquired. She does not understand many of the written instructions, and there is no dependable source of help after school. The report card records the answers she could produce. It does not record the teaching she did not receive.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: Payal loves drawing. She copies pictures from packaging, calendars and schoolbooks, noticing shapes and details other children miss. Her siblings save scraps of paper for her. Drawing is something she chooses to practise and something the family recognises she does well.

She remains enrolled, her parents want her to continue, and she has a clear interest a teacher could build on. What she lacks is sustained instruction at her current reading level. Moving her to a different section does not create that instruction automatically.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Payal continues attending after the transfer. Her new teacher asks her to describe one of her drawings and notices the difference between her spoken explanation and written work. Short reading sessions begin, using simple words alongside pictures. Her progress is gradual. The family still needs money, and as she approaches the end of primary school, her older siblings' earnings make starting work feel like a real alternative. Her continued schooling remains a question, not a settled outcome.

update: Payal has begun short reading sessions using pictures. The family’s income remains uncertain, and continued attendance will still need practical support.

name: Naveen

report.title: Home and family
paragraphs: Naveen lives with his parents and three siblings. His father works as a helper at a market and his mother cleans homes. The household receives roughly ₹6,000–₹9,000 a month. The children share one room and take turns using a small table. An older brother has begun working.

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has had breaks in attendance and cannot independently read much of the English text used in class. He copies from classmates rather than ask them to explain again. His parents want him to study but cannot read enough of his books to teach him at home.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes drawing cricket players and remembers their scores. His brother sometimes helps with sums. He needs regular reading practice and lessons that do not depend on private tuition the family cannot afford.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Naveen remains enrolled after transfer. The older brother’s earnings make work seem attractive, but he continues coming for now. Keeping him learning requires more than keeping his name on the attendance list.

update: Naveen is attending for now. His older brother’s earnings make work feel like an alternative. There is no individual reading plan in the office file.

name: Sara

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: She reads familiar lines and struggles when vocabulary changes. She can explain an idea after hearing it but needs support putting that explanation into writing. Her work is sometimes marked incomplete without identifying which part prevented her from starting.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: She likes making up conversations for paper puppets. She has adults who encourage her, though not the specific teaching help she needs. Working from an oral explanation towards a short written answer could show where she gets stuck.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Sara continues at school after transfer. She can speak more easily in class, but writing remains slow. A teacher begins using her spoken answers to plan what to practise next.

update: Sara is attending. Her teacher has started from spoken explanations before asking for writing, though progress remains gradual.

name: Rahul

report.title: Home and family

report.title: School and learning
paragraphs: He has strong recall and fairly high marks. He finds some explanations hard to follow but rarely says so. Being known as a good student makes him reluctant to hand in an unfinished attempt. He sometimes copies a method rather than reveal that he needs another explanation.

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes making rule sheets for playground games. The family provides books and attention. A classroom where questions are welcome would help him show uncertainty before it becomes a larger gap.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story
paragraphs: Rahul stays enrolled after transfer. He worries about how the decision will be explained at home. His skills remain, but rebuilding confidence and asking for help take time.

update: Rahul continues studying. He has begun asking questions in the new section. His family reports that he still worries about disappointing the school.

report.title: School and learning

name: Harish

report.title: School and learning

report.title: Interests and available support
paragraphs: He likes drawing machines and making quizzes for friends. He has someone available when he cannot understand a question. He would benefit from chances to explore answers that cannot be memorised beforehand.

report.title: Later, in this fictional story

update: Harish continues at school. His family questions the move, and his teacher reports that he needs reassurance as well as academic work.
